articles.title: New Scientist readers on how the magazine has shaped their lives
articles.content:
The first issue of New Scientist was published on 22 November 1956, and some of our readers have been with us since the very beginning. We asked subscribers, young and old, to tell us how they first encountered the magazine and how New Scientist has influenced their lives.
The volume of responses and the gratitude expressed within them were quite overwhelming. Here are some of our favourites, featuring a spectacular maggot experiment, science-inspired poetry and even a match made on the short-lived New Scientist dating site. Huge thanks to everyone who wrote in.
I was interested to see that New Scientist was launched “for all those men and women who are interested in scientific discovery and in its industrial, commercial and social consequences”. At the age of 13, I saved up a shilling from my Saturday morning “jobs” to purchase the first edition on 22 November 1956 and became one of those people interested in scientific discovery. Seventy years later, I remain a subscriber, after a scientific career that took me to many (if not, most!) countries in the world. New Scientist covered things like the opening of Jodrell Bank telescope in 1957. Since that was only about 50 miles (80 kilometres) away, it necessitated a bike ride to see what it really looked like! Peter Hall
Advertisement
I seem to have been reading New Scientist for the full 70! I do recall my encounter with the first edition: I was at Bec Grammar School in south London in a second-year physics class – it was 1956. The teacher, a genial boffin-type, announced the advent of the new publication and handed out copies – all I remember is its grey (or was it beige?) pages, which I read in a perfunctory way (I was only 12!) little thinking it would follow me through life and around the globe. Robyn Williams
I was at Malvern College in England for my O level examinations from 1955 to 1958. My science master at Malvern had recognised my interest in science and technology and he bought the very first issue of New Scientist with his own money. At the next science class, he stood up in front of the whole class and waved the first issue, saying, “Young Inman, a new UK science and technology magazine has been published and here is the first issue for you.” I went on to reach 60 years as a member of the UK Institution of Civil Engineers. Peter Inman
1956 puts me back at school – Fettes College in Edinburgh. The school adopted New Scientist from its first edition and it was available in the library, where senior boys interested in science were recommended to read it. And so began a lifetime of New Scientist – I have been a regular for as long as I can remember and a subscriber for a very long time. I am very grateful to New Scientist for maintaining my interest in all the sciences and new developments, which I am sure has helped me to think laterally and to have a greater understanding of what makes everything tick. Frank Evans
As a pupil in the mid-1960s at a girls’ grammar school in the north of England, one day I picked up a copy of New Scientist in the library. I was mind-blown by an article about Albert Einstein’s theories of relativity and time dilation, including a coloured diagram! I went on to study physical and material sciences at university and worked for eight years in research. But motherhood and misogyny (in those days before equal opportunities legislation) led me to change tack and I’ve been making pottery by hand for over 55 years. I like to think my science education hasn’t been wasted, but handed down to my daughters, one of whom reads New Scientist online in France. Every week, the paper issue landing on my doormat is devoured with excitement! Anne Rodgers
The stories that most interested me were about emerging electronics, the Sputnik satellite and the launch of Laika the space dog. The last of these prompted me to construct a module to house a maggot atop a 3-pence standard firework rocket and launch it. I later recovered the maggot unharmed and used it as fishing bait the next day. Mel
We are a group of 12 ladies “of a certain age” who meet once a month to discuss three or four articles from New Scientist. We tackle topics such as AI, quantum computing and cosmology – all of which are quite daunting! We persevere and continue to try to understand topics like these that are very challenging. We look up terms and concepts we don’t understand and then teach each other. We also love to read articles on climate change and medical science, as these feel more relatable. We plan to get the recordings of the talks from October’s New Scientist Live, so we can watch together and discuss. We want to thank you for making science accessible to us – we all feel that it’s important as we get older to not give in to the temptation to ignore all the new discoveries and changes in the world. Diana Currie, Dawn Segrue and the Marlow Science Group
An article about Benjamin Libet’s experiments in the 1980s showing there was a time gap between the brain making a decision and conscious awareness of that decision inspired me, as a psychotherapist, to find a way of using that gap in the field of psychological therapy. Two years of exploration and testing later, I taught the first cohort of students, and now it is being employed by psychologists, counsellors, psychiatrists and psychotherapists all over the world. Terence Watts
On the eve of New Scientist’s 70th anniversary, newsroom legend Andy Coghlan reveals four of the most dramatic and surprising moments from his storied career
Back in 2019, I stumbled across an eye-catching magazine on the shelves of a Tesco store. The title-page article caught my eye: “Does this one microbe cause all these conditions… and does that mean we can beat them?” It was at that moment that I truly fell in love with biology. Years have passed, and I have since graduated with a science degree from the University of Edinburgh and am now a returning student at my alma mater pursuing a master of research postgraduate degree in life sciences.
One day, I aim to be able to contribute – even if just a little – to aiding humanity in its endless fight against malady and illness. All of my academic achievements thus far may very well not have been possible had it not been for that magazine that caught my eye, that day in August 2019. And for that, I quite literally owe New Scientist all my academic achievements, and all that I have done, to this day. Stephen Wang
I am 87 and have been reading New Scientist every week since October 1964. I still have a note from my grandson, Maximilian, from when he was 5 years old, thanking me for reading New Scientist with him. He is now studying biology at my one-time college, Merton, at the University of Oxford. In the meantime, he has already succeeded, while travelling with his mother in Amazonia, in identifying, describing, naming and publishing a new genus and species of damselfly. He and I continue to discuss issues like evolution together, though I am a classicist by training. Anthony J. Nieduszynski
Your magazine is vital to our family. It sparks many conversations at the kitchen table. Our 11-year-old grandson keeps beating us to the latest issue. Our 6-year-old grandson has been enthralled with the cover art since he was 3. I cut out the cartoons and post them on the fridge. They have become the “cartoon of the week”. Often my grandsons see details I didn’t even catch. Krystyna Rodriguez
From subconscious finger sniffing to rats driving cars, New Scientist staff have reported on many weird, wild or utterly bonkers discoveries and inventions in the 70 years since we began
I have been a reader for almost all the publication’s life, as I first started when I was studying for A level qualifications in 1959/60. The article that really got me was one about the trouble the UK Ministry of Defence was having with dolphins that disrupted its torpedo testing by racing the torpedoes and giving them nudges of encouragement or perhaps challenge, thus putting them off target. I was hooked. It settled my decision to study engineering and, about six years later, I was actually employed as an engineer, working in a team trying to design turbine blades with better efficiency. I am now 83 and retired (well almost), but I still read every issue from cover to cover. Bryan Wilson
We first met when I was 18. I liked you a lot, but didn’t subscribe until I started my modest career as a poet of science rhymes for children (2009). Your writers, including Graham Lawton, Michael Marshall and Leah Crane, inspired 26 of the 80 poems I had published in CSIRO’s children’s science magazine Double Helix in Australia (plus many other poetic creations). In 2021, you kindly published my poem Brassica Bonanza on your Almost the last word pages (9 January), and Frosty Window Pane made it into Almost the last word in 2023 (13 May). So, I feel like we are friends now as well as work colleagues. And somewhere within that timeframe, my regular New Scientist magazine became INDISPENSABLE for more personal reasons. You have become my safe substitute for cigarettes. Every time I take a break, you help me not crave those nicotine nasties with your enlightening prose. Please don’t leave me! Love, Celia Berrell
I met my husband, Simon, on your dating website in 2012. It took me 50 years to find him, and without your mag, I probably never would have. We are two halves of a whole, and have been happily married now for 11 years. He is my heart’s delight, he makes me laugh, wears cravats with his T-shirts and is altogether quirky, like me. I still read New Scientist every week, and hope to be reading it still for many years to come. The quality of articles is outstanding – one day I may even get to understand quantum physics! We both love Tom Gauld’s cartoons, and keep a selection of them on the wall in the toilet, to entertain visitors. Andrea Cohen
I was delighted when my question about whether anything eats wasps was published in The Last Word (29 January 2005), and even more so when there was a full page of answers. But I was amazed when my question featured in the title of the first New Scientist questions book later that year. Apparently, the book was one of that Christmas’s bestsellers. Not only that, but there were two consecutive reviews in The Times – pretty good for my complete published scientific writing! And what did I get out of this? The original answerers got 25 quid each. Me? Not a penny. Only a fleeting, obscure fame. Fair enough. A great science magazine for the ordinary folks like myself. I will not be cancelling my subscription. Tom Eastwood
I answered my first two Last Word questions in 1997, when the column was relatively new. Amusingly, both appeared in the same issue, something I gather the rules now prevent. I had always admired New Scientist, but never quite imagined it would publish anything I might write – perhaps a touch of imposter syndrome. Nearly 30 years later, I’m still providing answers. I particularly enjoy questions requiring a back-of-the-envelope calculation or a little mathematical modelling. I like getting absorbed in a problem and trying to explain a tricky concept clearly and concisely. It is one of the few ways I experience mindfulness.
Some questions have spun off in unexpected directions. One, about whether pigeons sweat, led to an email while I was scuba-diving in Thailand asking me to appear on the TV programme BBC Breakfast. Answers have also developed into articles elsewhere, sometimes after reading somebody else’s answer and questioning my own. My favourite? Like the Eye of Sauron, my focus is always on the one I’m looking at right now. Mike Follows

articles.title: Noise pollution is reshaping the health and behaviour of animals everywhere
articles.content:
If you listen closely to an underwater seagrass meadow, you can hear the actual sound of photosynthesis. During the day, tiny bubbles of oxygen float from the blades of the seagrass to the ocean’s surface. The popping sound these bubbles make when they burst is like “tinkling bells”, according to Carlos Duarte, a keen scuba diver and expert on ocean noise at the King Abdullah University of Science and Technology in Saudi Arabia.
“As long as the meadows are more than 2 metres beneath the ocean surface, when the bubbles break they generate a vibration that is in the same sound frequency as bells,” he says. “If you have a hydrophone and you quantify this, then you could even calculate photosynthetic rates.”
But most of the time, this remarkable acoustic phenomenon is drowned out by human-caused noise pollution. There is barely a habitat on Earth that isn’t subjected to anthropogenic noise pollution from boats, cars, aeroplanes or any number of other noisy human activities. In the oceans, ambient noise levels are about 10 times higher than they were in 1950. “To understand the impact of noise on the marine environment, we need to imagine ourselves living in a great party, 24/7, throughout our entire lifespan. It is really a persistent and chronic impact,” says Duarte.
Advertisement
Now, scientists are learning more about how serious and widespread the impact of noise pollution is on wildlife subjected to it – and the results are disturbing. A meta-analysis published in the journal Science earlier this month looked at 214 experimental studies on 177 aquatic and terrestrial species, spanning six continents. It concluded that noise pollution altered at least one physiological, developmental or behavioural trait in 80 per cent of the species studied, with the effects occurring in every habitat. In short, noise pollution is reshaping the health and behaviour of a huge range of animals across land and sea.
“Every ecosystem, or every major habitat, is affected by noise,” says Hansjoerg Kunc at Queen’s University Belfast in the UK, who conducted the analysis with his colleague Rouven Schmidt. “We looked at a lot of different physiological responses [in wildlife] and basically nearly all of them found an effect for noise.”
In general, noise forces predators to work 2.5 times harder to catch 25 per cent less prey overall, reported Kunc and Schmidt. Creatures like bats expend more energy and are less successful at hunting when subjected to ambient noise, while noise from ship engines disrupts communication and disorientates marine life such as whales and dolphins.
Animals also learn to avoid noisy habitats, which shrinks their available area and therefore limits their population size. Dolphins, for example, actively avoid noisy coastlines, while bats have been shown to avoid roads that were noisy during a motorcycle rally long after the vehicles had left the area.
In noise-polluted areas, mortality among animals studied jumped by 138 per cent, on average. Sometimes, the death is instantaneous: underwater explosions from oil and gas exploration, for example, can cause a fish’s bladder to explode. Other times, it is slower and more painful, such as gradual starvation from reduced hunting success.
Not every animal suffers a negative impact from noise pollution, Kunc notes. Some predators might benefit from noise – enjoying increased hunting success when human noise flushes their prey out of its hiding place, for example.
But even though some animals might benefit in the short term, the overall effect is negative on the ecosystem, he says, because its natural dynamics are being warped by external stress. “If you think about an ecosystem, all species in this ecosystem have adapted to the way it should be,” he says. “So, from my point of view, it doesn’t really matter who is more affected or less affected. It is changing, and that is what we want to avoid, because we want to protect a functioning ecosystem.”
Kunc wants more thought to be given to protecting the soundscape of the natural world, alongside the conservation of physical habitats. “We know that the acoustic environment is a strong evolutionary force, and we have shown that it really changes the physiology, development and behaviour [of wildlife],” he says.
Some efforts are already under way. In the US, national parks such as Yellowstone have designated quiet zones, which reduce the amount of noise made by visitors by 3 to 5 decibels according to Rachel Buxton, formerly of the US National Parks Service and now at Carleton University in Canada.
She thinks more can be done to reduce noise pollution, especially in protected areas, such as by closing roads to traffic during certain periods or re-routing aircraft to shadow busy road networks and avoid wilderness areas.
“Think of the Grand Canyon. We wouldn’t dream of building a giant building in the middle of the Grand Canyon, and yet there are overflight tours that pass over the airspace all the time, polluting the whole space with noise,” she points out.
Pitcairn Island, one of the remotest places on Earth, was once home to mutineers. Today it’s a trailblazer in biodiversity protection with lessons for us all
We also need to tackle noise pollution at sea, says Duarte. He argues for enforcing acoustic limits in marine protected areas, which could include setting noise limits for ships and other marine activities.
New technologies also give hope for a quieter future. Emerging evidence suggests that electric vehicles are quieter and therefore less disturbing to most wildlife. Similarly, electric motorboats and ferries could lead to quieter shorelines for marine life, says Duarte. “Moving to electric mobility, which we’ve done largely on land, to the ocean will immediately reduce noise around the shorelines,” he says, pointing out that countries such as Sweden are leading the way in creating a market for electric boats.
The covid-19 pandemic offers an insight into what happens in the natural world when the noise stops. Noise pollution across oceans dropped by 20 per cent during the crisis, says Duarte, and led to extraordinary sightings of marine life returning to busy waterways and city shorelines, and the sound of birdsong filling cities.
Unlike pollutants that linger in the atmosphere, shutting off the noise immediately removes the problem, Duarte points out. “As soon as the noise stops, then animals claim back their ancestral territory and home,” he says.
articles.summary: There is almost nowhere on Earth free from disruptive human noise – but it's one of the easiest environmental problems to solve

articles.title: Did El Niño cause an early breakdown in the polar vortex?
articles.content:
The polar vortex has suffered an unprecedented early breakdown, threatening Europe with cold and snow, and some scientists think the record super El Niño is to blame.
The polar vortex, a high-altitude band of westerly winds circling the Arctic that bottles up cold air over the north pole, typically strengthens through the winter and weakens in the spring.
The El Niño climate phase, which has already warmed surface waters in the tropical Pacific to record temperatures and continues to heat up, tends to keep the vortex strong in autumn and early winter. Then, in late winter, it often weakens the vortex, allowing that cold air to spill southwards into Europe and sometimes North America.
Advertisement
But on 10 November, the polar vortex weakened to the point that it broke down, with the winds reversing direction to blow weakly from the east. While these collapses happen every few years, they almost never occur in November. This is the earliest it has happened since weather balloon records began in the 1950s, beating the old record by 18 days.
This may have been due to random fluctuations in the atmosphere. It is also possible, however, that the extremely strong El Niño could have sped up the weakening of the polar vortex that typically happens later in the winter, though that isn’t proven, according to Adam Scaife at the Met Office, the UK’s weather service.
“There probably is some kind of El Niño influence on it,” he says. “That would be my suspicion, but we don’t know that for sure.”
As east-to-west trade winds weaken during El Niño and the warm water they built up in the western Pacific washes back eastwards, a low-pressure centre of warm, rising air moves eastwards with it. This causes extra waviness in the jet stream, another band of strong westerly winds that circles the globe, except further south and lower in the atmosphere than the polar vortex. The jet stream meanders further southwards around Alaska, deepening a low-pressure system there called the Aleutian low.
But the El Niño-linked wave doesn’t just propagate side to side in the jet stream. It can also propagate upwards into the stratosphere, where the polar vortex is. As the air gets thinner, the wave’s amplitude gets bigger until it crashes into the polar vortex like a wave crashing onto a beach, says Scaife. And while the polar vortex is westerly, these waves carry easterly momentum.
“When they dump that momentum, they push the polar vortex against its flow, and they weaken it,” he says.
But another reason for the polar vortex breakdown could be a high-pressure “blocking” system that developed over Scandinavia in recent weeks, which blocked the jet stream and caused large meanders in it. This waviness could also have weakened the polar vortex through the same wave-breaking process, regardless of El Niño.
“I would be wary of saying it was caused by El Niño,” says Andrew Charlton-Perez at the University of Reading, UK. “I would say the blocking high is probably more important.”
The reversal of the polar vortex isn’t related to the current cold weather in the UK. But it could bring even more cold, snowy weather in the coming weeks.
A polar vortex breakdown is also known as a sudden stratospheric warming event. As the winds weaken, high-level air rushes in over the north pole, increasing atmospheric pressure and raising temperatures, just as pumping up a bike tyre warms it up.
Meanwhile, over the following weeks, cold surface-level air can descend from the Arctic into northern Europe. A polar vortex breakdown preceded the “Beast from the East” cold snap in 2018, when blizzards covered much of the UK in snow and killed 10 people.
While the polar vortex is expected to strengthen towards the end of November, bringing warmer weather, it could break down again this winter, Scaife warns.
“The risk of cold easterlies this winter is increasing,” he says.
articles.summary: The polar vortex winds have undergone an unprecedented weakening, which could bring cold weather to Europe. Some scientists suspect the record El Niño is to blame

articles.title: Researchers build the first ever quantum clock that uses sunlight
articles.content:
For the first time, researchers have built a quantum clock that uses light from the sun as a key component. It could be used to diagnose shifts in the sun’s velocity or probe processes on its surface.
This is not your mother’s sundial. People have known that they can keep track of time with sunlight ever since antiquity. But contemporary record-breaking timekeepers, which are called optical clocks, derive their accuracy from quantum mechanical effects and typically have atoms that have been isolated from the external world at their core. Now, Scott Diddams at the University of Colorado, Boulder, and his colleagues have built an optical clock that relies on sunlight instead.
In a typical optical clock, an electron within an atom is made to oscillate between two energy levels, and an ultra-stable laser is tuned, or locked, to the frequency of that oscillation. Next, these oscillations – the ups and downs of the light waves that comprise the laser beam – are translated into usable ticks of a clock. To do this, researchers use a device called a frequency comb, which turns visible light into microwaves that can be processed by standard electronics.
Advertisement
In the new experiment, the researchers still used a laser and a frequency comb to build their clock, but the role of the atom was played by a process that happens near the sun.
Specifically, instead of locking their laser to an electron’s jumps within an atom, the researchers locked it to a process where sunlight causes similar jumps as it hits iron atoms in our star’s atmosphere. This process leaves a signature in the spectrum of colours that comprise sunlight, so the team collected sunlight into a special fibre and fed it into the rest of the clock. This type of solar optical clock has never been built before.
While the new clock doesn’t rival the best atomic optical clocks in accuracy, the researchers showed that it could possibly be used as a tool for studying stars. During the partial solar eclipse in 2024, they observed a signature shift in the sunlight’s spectrum due to the moon passing in front of the star. If the clock was fed light from a faraway star in place of sunlight, similar shifts could indicate the presence of orbiting exoplanets, which raises the possibility of the new clock design becoming a tool for astronomical discovery. In this case, however, starlight would have to be collected through large telescopes, sometimes over long periods of time.
Researchers have designed a quantum version of a pendulum clock. It could shed light on timekeeping in the quantum realm
Piet Schmidt at the National Metrology Institute of Germany says that the new work is interesting because it demonstrates an optical clock design that leverages light from the stars rather than being based exclusively on objects under tight control in the lab.
But as an astronomical instrument, it doesn’t yet surpass existing methods for studying light from stars, and for very distant stars, the new clock’s usefulness would be seriously limited by how faint their light is, says Schmidt.
There may, however, be advantages in studying the properties of our sun, he says. For example, the clock could probe eruptive events, sunspots and the effects of solar “wind” made from streams of charged particles in the outer layers of the sun’s atmosphere.
articles.summary: Quantum clocks usually rely on advanced lasers and isolated atoms in the lab, but a new experiment showed that the same clock design can work with sunlight instead

articles.title: Which science-fiction novels have been best at predicting the future?
articles.content:
New Scientist has always been interested in science fiction and its attempts to imagine the future. In 1958, when the magazine was 2 years old, it published an article by Ian S. Menzies in which he wrote: “Like every other form of literature, s. f. ranges from excellent to awful. But the best of science fiction today is far superior to much other fiction.” Elsewhere in the feature, Menzies talked about the risks of the “rapid catching up of reality with fiction”.
It’s true that some of the sci-fi he was reading then was rapidly overtaken by events and, in the process of that, rendered redundant. What Menzies couldn’t know was that other works from that same period would still be regarded as prescient, important or relevant, or even all three, decades later.
So, which sci-fi stories, published over the seven decades of New Scientist’s history, have proved to be both prophetic and enduringly pertinent as the world has changed around them? Here are some of my personal picks.
Advertisement
The 1950s
The Death of Grass by John Christopher (1956) is an English period piece, with all the particular social politics of its era on display (sexism included). Yet somehow it manages to foreshadow a host of modern-day crises, from pandemics and the fragility of food supply lines to the befouling and stripping of the land by big agriculture.
The book opens with the news that a virus is killing grasses; eventually that comes to include all cereal crops. Abruptly, the country’s food reserves are gone, and no more food is coming. The novel’s main characters are mostly middle-class professionals who do a few things “right” early on. They are quick to acquire guns and flee London; also, quick to gun down anyone who tries to stop them. They make their way in convoy through a brown land, heading towards a Cumbrian valley where one of their group has a relative. The valley is gated; one way in, one way out. They think they could be safe there.
First they have to survive their journey, though, and England, within hours, is lawless. I finished the book wishing that I could buy a remote valley and build a wall across the bottom of it.
The 1960s
The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress by Robert A. Heinlein (1966) is the story, set in 2075, of a group of lunar residents who plot to overthrow their overlords on Earth. It’s a great premise rendered quite dull in execution; much of the book reads like the minutes from a local council meeting. In addition, the sexual politics of the colony are filtered through male 1960s sensibilities, adding cringeworthy moments.
The reason this remains a classic is that one of the characters in the book, Mike, is an AI. Not just some 60s idea of what an AI might be, but our idea of an AI. On the very first page, our narrator Mannie (who speaks a futuristic version of English) writes: “Mike was a fair dinkum thinkum, sharpest computer you’ll ever meet… Not that Mike would necessarily give right answer; he wasn’t completely honest.” Remind you of anything?
The 1970s
Ursula K. Le Guin’s astonishing novel The Dispossessed (1974) remains daisy fresh. Le Guin, as her fans will know, could do it all: character, politics, ideas, exquisite writing… and, in this case, spaceships too.
Our hero, Shevek, is a brilliant physicist and also a good man (what a wonderful creation he is!) trying to do right in a future where the human colonies have gone different ways – one into anarchy, for example, another into the rule of an elite – as they struggle with climate change, moral exhaustion, repression, inequality… and much else that we struggle with today. If you’ve never read this one, I highly recommend it.
The 1980s
In Atwood’s masterwork, the US has been captured by a radical right-wing group and is now called the Republic of Gilead. Women’s rights have been scrapped. Our hero, named Offred by the new regime, is assigned as a handmaid to a family of loyalists. Her job is to produce a baby for the commander who is her new master. She is, in short, a womb with arms and legs, and nothing more, to Gilead.
I don’t think I need to draw any lines for you, straight or otherwise, from this book written 40 years ago to current events.
Atwood aside, I didn’t want to leave out Neuromancer because its vision of our digital future is so weirdly prescient. Gibson, famously, was no computer expert and wrote the book on a typewriter. Yet he foresaw what cyberspace would actually be like.
Case, our chief protagonist, is a former hacker trying to make ends meet in Japan after his ability to access cyberspace has been taken from him. Then a woman called Molly approaches him, asking him to get involved in a heist. Cue a high-stakes drama in and out of cyberspace. The book is a bit dense to start with, but it’s well worth sticking with.
The 1990s
Octavia E. Butler’s Parable of the Sower (1993) is a barnstormer of a novel that remains as relevant today as when it was first published. Our hero, Lauren Olamina, is a young woman living in a gated community in a United States that is rapidly falling apart.
Climate change is escalating and the streets are full of desperate people forced into savagery simply to survive. Lauren’s community is hanging on, but soon the chaos is going to come through that gate.
Lauren, still a teenager, develops her own religion and names it Earthseed. Its divine purpose is for humans to colonise the stars. Such a bold vision is preposterous amidst the horror of the world Lauren is forced to make her way through, and yet it sustains her.
The book is a hymn (I think) to the power of taking full responsibility for your life and facing up to the fact that everything changes. Let us hope, as with The Death of Grass, that this version of the future remains in some parts fictional.
Butler wrote a follow-up, Parable of the Talents, in which Lauren sees her dreams begin to come true. A third book in the series remained unfinished when Butler died.
The 2000s
One does need some time to pass before being able to decide if a book has truly got the future right. However, I am reasonably confident that The Three-Body Problem by Cixin Liu (2008) is going to prove to be so.
The story is a brilliant one. Aliens are heading for Earth, and they’re not friendly, but it’s going to take them hundreds of years to arrive. Can the scientists of Earth band together and push science forward so hard that humans will survive the coming invasion? Yes, Liu wrote a book all about physics, but made it gripping!
So, in the case of the book, the science push is all about aliens. But it doesn’t take a big leap of the imagination to suggest that there might be some important real world parallels here. This is the first of a trilogy. The two follow-up novels are also fantastic.
The 2010s and beyond…
I’m going to take a chance on two very different novels from recent times that might, in the future, be viewed as accurate visions.
First, Station Eleven (2014) by Emily St. John Mandel, which essentially predicted the covid-19 pandemic. Except in Mandel’s pandemic, the world was left in ruins.
We follow a travelling group of actors and musicians as they journey between communities in this future world. The book explores the idea that “survival is insufficient”; that humanity needs art, culture and history to truly live. Its ideas still feel extremely relevant 12 years later.
Second, Kim Stanley Robinson’s chronicle of the near future, The Ministry for the Future (2020). Clear-eyed, but essentially optimistic, it describes humanity’s efforts to deal with climate change in the decades to come.
This is a very untraditional book in structure, and although you could say the main character is Mary Murphy, the head of the titular ministry, parts of the book are devoted to (fictional) witness accounts of future events. It’s not an easy read, but then it’s not an easy subject, and this is a massively ambitious work.
Despite the horrors contained in the book, we may end up wishing, in the future, that it had been more prescient, rather than less.
So those are my picks. You may have better ones. In terms of Ian S. Menzies’s central argument seven long decades ago, I think that what he said still holds true. Science fiction continues to range from excellent to awful. But the best of sci-fi today is still far superior to much other fiction. It’s where the big ideas are, simple as that.
Did Emily get it right? Come and join the discussion about the sci-fi novels that have best predicted the future
Emily H. Wilson is author of the Sumerians series and is working on her first sci-fi novel. She is a former editor of New Scientist, and is now the magazine’s science-fiction columnist
articles.summary: We’ve loved sci-fi at New Scientist for the past 70 years, but which novels got the future right? From Neuromancer to The Handmaid’s Tale, Emily H. Wilson picks the most prescient reads of the past seven decades
